INTRODUCTION

In modern times, the family has suffered the attack of the transformations within society and culture more than any other institution. Some people have remained faithful to the values which lay the foundation for the family; others, however, have allowed themselves to be won over by uncertainty and discouragement. Still others walk in doubt or ignorance of their own nature and mission. It is the mission of the Church, Mother not only of individuals but also of all Christian families, to lead those families to the Light of Eternal Life: some families she must sustain, others she must illumine, and the rest she must help along the path on which they walk blindly, groping as they try find their way in this world.

In this book, we reproduce two works by Father Carlos M. Buela, IVE. The first article is entitled “Modern Attacks Against the Family,” first published in the magazine Mikael in 1975 and subsequently in an offprint of the same Editorial, which was soldout, updated, and sold-out once again, a clear indication of its great acceptance and use by families.1 Over thirty-five years later, its value has by no means decreased; on the contrary, today more than ever, marriages and families need to know themselves in order to accomplish their mission in the world. They must know not only their essence, their end, their prerogatives, their gifts, but also the enemies who threaten them, perhaps more than at any other time in history. In order for the family to do what Blessed Pope John Paul II wrote in his Apostolic Exhortation Familiaris Consortio, “Family, become what you are!,”2 the family must—before all else— learn what it is.

The second article, entitled “Catholic Courtship,” appeared in the magazine Diálogo, supplementing the previous topic with the author’s keen reflections on this important stage which prepares a couple for marriage and which, in many cases, decides their future.3 In these pages, Fr. Buela has poured forth a great deal of his pastoral experience with young couples, many of whom he accompanied in their preparation for the sacrament of Marriage. In this article, you will find the sure guides of morality and spirituality for a relationship based in love for Christ and for the Church and also in the great gift that is the preparation itself.

Together with the first article, this second helps us to recognize what Blessed Pope John Paul II, in his second encounter with families in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), said: “The well-being of the individual person and of human and Christian society is intimately linked with the healthy condition of that community produced by marriage and family.”4

In the same vein, this Pope, when dedicating his Exhortation Familiaris Consortio to families, said, “To you married couples; to you, fathers and mothers of families; to you, young men and women, the future and the hope of the Church and of the world, destined to be the dynamic central nucleus of the family in the approaching third millennium; to you, venerable and dear Brothers in the Episcopate and in the priesthood, beloved sons and daughters in the religious life, souls consecrated to the Lord, who bear witness to married couples to the ultimate reality of the love of God; to you, upright men and women. . . . The future of humanity passes by way of the family. It is therefore indispensible and urgent that

MODERN ATACKS AGAINST THE FAMILY

A TEXT FOR PASTORAL WORK WITH MARRIAGES

AND FAMILIES

Before our very eyes, already anesthetized by habit, there is an attempt to destroy everything that pertains to the natural order with the morbid hope that, once the foundations on which the supernatural order rests are removed, that order will also be destroyed.

In recent times, there has been a notable and particular determination to destroy the family, the “cell of society”6 and the domestic Church7; these efforts have the foolish goal of pulling society and the Church down into ruins, and this because it is in the church of the family that people learn to love God, their nation, and their neighbor. It is only in healthy families—and only exceptionally outside of them—that strong and virtuous men and women are formed, heroes and saints, who are the only ones able to build up their nation and to sow the seed of the Church, even with their own blood if necessary.

The family currently suffers a wide range of attacks, ranging from attacks from those who openly intend to destroy the institution of the family, to those who entangle it with thousands of sophisms in order to dissolve and weaken it, or even to deny it its proper place as something of fundamental importance, as is done, for example, by Fr. André Aubry, O.P., who maintains that, “No matter how indispensible it may be, it [the family] is no longer is the basic cell of society.”8

In this short work, we’ll try to see the principle fronts on which the Catholic family is systematically assailed. There are five such fronts:

1) The essence of the marriage

2) The ends of the marriage 3) Authority with regard to the family 4) Responsible Parenthood 5) Love In each of these aspects, we can offer numerous examples— including examples from within the realm of “Catholic” thinkers— of the work that dissolves and subverts the natural and supernatural order, a work brought about by the modern emulators of Voltaire, Rousseau, Freud, Marx, Marcuse, and company.

1.

THE ESSENCE OF MARRIAGE

God Himself is the Author of the family and He Himself is the One who restores it, since He elevated it to the category and dignity of a sacrament. This means that the family is not merely a human institution, but rather something of divine institution; hence, it is not subject to the subjective and inconsistent whims of men, since marriage participates, in some measure, in the immutability of God Himself, with respect to its nature, ends, and laws. These cannot be any nature, ends, or laws other than those given by God Himself, the Author and Restorer of the family.

In a few words, we could say that the essence of Catholic marriage is the society formed by mutual consent, given before God, of “ONE MAN WITH ONE WOMAN FOREVER”9.

Against this natural and divine order—“one man to one woman forever”—we can point out six main destructions:

6 LAY “MARRIAGE”

The last destruction against the natural and divine order is put forward by a few baptized who think that the marriage of one man and one woman with consent given before each other, appropriately called “lay marriage,” is valid. What this “marriage” does is simply secularize and desecrate the sacred reality of Catholic marriage. Those who support this as valid give themselves the ability to alter the essence and laws of the institution of the family as though God, the Supreme Legislator, and the Church, His faithful interpreter, had no absolute obligations or rights over it.

These are, in broad strokes, the six deviations which distort the very nature of the natural contract that has been elevated to the dignity of sacrament, in which “one man and one woman” are united forever before God.

2.

THE ENDS OF MARRIAGE

The essential and complementary ends of marriage are:

The procreation and education of children, and The manifestation of mutual love.

That both ends are essential doesn’t mean that there is no subordination between them, since it is impossible for one thing to have several last ends.

The primary essential end is that of the procreation and education of offspring, and the secondary essential ends are “mutual aid, the cultivating of mutual love, and the quieting of concupiscence.”17 Pope Pius XII clearly teaches that the secondary ends, “inasmuch as they are intended by nature, are not equally primary, much less superior to the primary end, but are essentially subordinated to it.”18

Although some may not use these exact words, consecrated by the Church’s Magisterium, if they want to remain within Catholic doctrine, they are obligated, whether they like it or not, to recognize the reality that those words transmit.

Others, claiming to base themselves in the Second Vatican Council, attempt to whittle away or alter the essential subordination between these two ends of matrimony, placing love before procreation. Whoever supports such claims only shows their ignorance of the conciliar documents.

According to Pope Paul VI, the teachings of Vatican II are always to be understood on the same line as “previous ecclesial Magisterium,” of which the Council is nothing more than a “continuation, explanation, and growth.”19

Furthermore, the Second Vatican Council’s Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes, in the chapter entitled “Fostering the Nobility of Marriage and the Family,” cites Pope Pius XI’s 1930 encyclical Casti Connubii, the fundamental encyclical on Christian Marriage, five times as in accord with its teaching. With regard to the “various ends” of marriage, paragraph 48 of Gaudium et Spes has a footnote referring to Saint Augustine, Saint Thomas, and the encyclical Casti Connubii, where the subordination of those ends is explicitly affirmed.

Thus, if the Second Vatican Council cites previous documents of the Church’s Magisterium in its support, it’s also because that

Council endorses the doctrine that the early documents contain, and it couldn’t be any other way, since anything else would be logically incoherent and completely absurd.

3 TWO ESSENTIAL ENDS: COMPLIMEN- TARY BUT SUBORDINATED

We must affirm with all of our strength, together with the Magisterium of every generation, that the essential ends of marriage do not exclude but rather complement each other in the primacy of procreation and education of children above mutual love. This is a truth that is so rooted in the very nature of marriage and so explicit in God’s Law that the Angelic Doctor teaches:

“Nor, in fact, should it be deemed a slight sin for a man to arrange for the emission of semen apart from the proper purpose of generating and bringing up children. . . . After the sin of homicide whereby a human nature already in existence is destroyed, this type of sin appears to take next place, for by it the generation of human nature is precluded.”27

However, it must also be said that if there is a mistake made “in excess,” that is, in exalting love as the primary end, there is also a mistake “in deficiency,” by removing the loving character of this essential—though secondary—end, as if the sole end of marriage was the procreation and education of children.

3.

AUTHORITY IN THE FAMILY

Authority is not anything bad, but rather good and “very good”31 as long as it comes from God, as Our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to Pilate:

“You would have no power over me if it had not been given to you from above,” (Jn 19:11). As Saint Paul teaches:

“Let every person be subordinate to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore, whoever resists authority opposes what God has appointed, and those who oppose it will bring judgment upon themselves” (Rom 13:1-2).

Therefore, authority in the family should be respected, honored, and obeyed as done “for the Lord and not for others” (Col 3:23).

a) Opinions about authority in the family

-Some assert that all authority is bad, and so they fight against it, like anarchists;

-Others maintain that it needs to disappear, like some liberals;

-The Marxists say that it is alienating (wherever they aren’t the ones in charge)32;

-For Freudians, it is fruit of the Oedipus complex; -The followers of Rousseau claim that authority originates in the free consent of family members;

-Others dilute it into mere empty service, in which the only things done are what the masses want; this is what happens in civil or even ecclesiastical demagogic democracy that seeks only to “flatter the ears” (cf. 2 Tim 4:4).

This is because modern man in general rebels “against any form of authority or of preeminence, against any dominating structure.”33 As Chesterton says, “in the act of destroying the idea of

Divine authority we have largely destroyed the idea of that human authority.”34

b) The Church’s Doctrine

The Catholic doctrine of authority in the family is very different from the views espoused above: “The authority of fathers of families preserves a certain impressed image and form of the authority which is in God, ‘of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named’ (Eph 3:15).”35

Jesus teaches that whoever has authority must serve, but not in some position lower to a doormat, but rather as a father, in the bosom of the family.

c) The undermining of authority in the family

The degree to which authority in the family has been undermined is quite serious. Let’s examine this on three levels: with respect to parents, to spouses, and to children.

1 THE AUTHORITY OF PARENTS

Now-a-days, it’s common to see parents who entirely refrain from giving commands or laying down rules. With the excuse of wanting to be friends with their child (which is not bad in itself), the parent becomes a best-friend, buddy, or pal, and even accomplice or partner-in-crime—and this is very bad.

Parents have become incapable of punishing and, for the most part, powerless to educate, since man is educated by being rewarded for what he does right and punished for what he does wrong.

Just as there is an entire campaign against authority in the family, because it comes from God and because authority is needed so that the community might not “come to dissolution and be prevented from attaining the end for which it was created and instituted,”36 there is also an entire campaign against the healthy exercise of authority, like the prudent punishment of faults.

Since authority is not something bad, neither is the just exercise of authority. Pope Leo XIII teaches that “this authority taken from God not only takes its origin and force from Him, but also borrows its nature and character. Hence, the Apostle exhorts children to ‘obey their parents in the Lord, and honor their father and mother, which is the first commandment with promise’ (Ef 6,1–2).”37

a) Educational Correction

When correction and punishment are done in a prudent and balanced way, they become powerful tools of education. It’s useful to keep in mind that old saying:

“If one look suffices for correction, don’t make a gesture; If a gesture suffices, don’t say a single word; If a single word suffices, don’t raise your voice; If raising your voice suffices, don’t give a punishment...”

The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews asks himself, “For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?” (Heb 12:7).

Elsewhere, the Holy Spirit teaches, “He who spares his son the rod hates his son, but he who loves him takes care to chastise him” (Prv 13:24).

Clearly punishment should be proportionate to the fault and it’s better that it be too little than too much. After making the child aware of what he has done wrong, it is very beneficial to ask him what punishment he deserves. The child, who has a great sense of justice, generally imposes upon himself a greater punishment than his father would. This is where the father should take advantage of the occasion to decrease the punishment, joining mercy with justice.

The punishment shouldn’t last very long, but it must be opportunely applied: if it’s not given at the moment given, it would be better not to apply it at all than to apply it later. Above all, however, the punishment should be medicinal, that is, it should remedy the problem and not worsen it. For the most part, if the parent is irate, it would be best to hold off punishing because it will be excessive, rendering the educative power of correction useless. This is because the punishment will no longer spring from paternal love for the child’s well-being, but rather from a bad mood or from agitation which color punishment with a tinge of revenge, spite, and even egoism.

This is understandable because, according to St. Thomas, the family is the second womb.40 Just as man needs the first to exist, be nourished, have a favorable “atmosphere,” to be protected and to develop, normally he also needs a family to exist, to survive, to mature as a human person, to nourish his spirit with the learning of all virtues, to not prematurely expose himself to the dangers that await him in his public life, and in fewer words: to learn to live and to love.

Once those sacred bonds which unite children to their parents in the flesh have been destroyed, it becomes very easy to destroy the sacred bonds that unite the child of God by adoption with his Heavenly Father. St. Paul also points out that one can walk the road going the wrong way like those who, on account of their denial of God, God

This entire campaign against filial obedience is made concrete in hundreds of fallacious slogans, repeated here and there, in different forms but with the same end. These are just a few among many:

a) The parents’ defects:

In no way are children excused from filial obligations because their parents don’t have a primary or high school school education: many didn’t have the opportunity to study, and those who are embarrassed by their parents should always remember that if they know anything at all, they owe it to their parents’ sacrifices.

LOVE

One of the perverse fruits of a revolutionary-bourgeois society, exacerbated by the propaganda in a Marxist society, is the elimination of hierarchy from everything and everyone, leveling all things upon the same playing field.

This plebeianism, which denies every distinction and seniority, is the enemy of every healthy hierarchy; it has also been introduced into the heart of our families and, above all, into that which constitutes its essence: love.

Such plebeianism produces a crude equalitarianism that leads all love to its ruin by claiming to reduce it to a common denominator.

This destructive attack on families is still more serious when it falls not only on an unhealthy and nonhierarchical mediocrity in love—i.e., loving your husband and children on the same equal plane—but also on the pending inclination towards a love that is anti-hierarchical—i.e. forgetting your husband for the love of your children.

On the contrary, when love is true, it comes from God, and everything that comes from God is “ordered” (Rom 13:1). For the most part, if love is true, it should necessarily be ordered, namely, it should present itself, as St. Augustine teaches, as an “order of love.”56 A mother should not have the same degree of love for her husband as she has for her children, her father, or for her sister-inlaw.

This hierarchy of love in the family comes about on account of good and of the degree of union:

On account of the good, parents hold a privileged place in the family’s love since they are the natural origin of their children; after God, children owe their very existence to their parents. Hence, parents are owed submission, love, and respect because “we are of their flesh.”

On account of the degree of union between the lover and the beloved, however, one’s spouse must be more loved, because “they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Mt 19:6). This is why “a man loves his wife more intensely, but his parents with greater reverence.”57

After one’s spouse, love for children is the next most intense, since children are a prolongation of the parents: “they are flesh of the flesh of their parents.” A child is closer to his or her parents since the child is a part of them, and they have loved him for longer. Any inversion in the order of love must be avoided. There are women who seem to have gotten married with their parents or with their children, and so do not give their husband that primacy of place that belongs to him. This could be the reason why the husband is happier at the bar with his friends than at home with his family. This disordered love acts against the very reality of life itself, since children normally get married and go on to form their own families, while the husband is the one who will remain with his wife until death separates them.

Lastly comes the love of siblings: “we are of the same flesh,” and love for other relatives.

We must defend our families from all of these enemies, since no matter how large, powerful, and wide-spread they might be, they will never be able to do more than God:

“If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rm 8:31).

Although we may have to live in the times of the Anti-Christ, we have the best defense prepared in the Passion of Christ, as Saint Thomas Aquinas teaches:

“There is always a remedy provided through Christ’s Passion, for defending themselves against the wicked snares of the demons, even in Antichrist’s time. But if any man neglects to make use of this remedy, it detracts nothing from the efficacy of Christ’s Passion.”77

Secondly, given the great negative influence that the world exercises on our families in these days, we must strengthen and intensify our educational works much more than before.

On the one hand, this is done by the parents giving an example of an authentic Christian life—particularly by fulfilling the Sunday obligation, frequenting the sacraments, and defending the Church’s teachings—since children generally will become what their parents are: this is evident with those parents who give bad examples, since they “do not attempt to correct their children of the sins which they also recognize in themselves.”78

On the other hand, this is done by educating children with correction and discipline. Saint Alphonsus says of those who neglect this duty:

“Were fathers or mothers to lead a life of piety and continual prayer, and to receive Holy Communion every day, they should be damned if they neglected the education of their children.”79

Parents should take care that their children do not form bad friendships, for “bad company corrupts good morals” (1 Cor 15:33).

They should also try to monitor what their children are taught in school, what books they read and the places they frequently go.

No expense of time and energy is too much when it is for the formation of those who will be the future of our nation and of our Church.

Thus, as the most complete subordination to the nature and to the ends of Catholic marriages and families, in each of our families we must promote healthy paternal and maternal authority, generosity in the transmission of life, and a respect for the order of love, cooperating with the grace given in the holy sacrament of marriage, for, as Saint Robert Bellarmine says, “matrimony . . . is a sacrament like to that of the Eucharist, which not only when it is being conferred, but also whilst it remains, is a sacrament.”80

In this difficult time in the history of the Church and of our nation, each one of our families must entirely commit themselves so as not to compromise on any Christian principles, to be forgers of the greatest and noblest deeds that the world has ever seen, because these deeds are what formed the great saints, of whom “the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).

Let us not be afraid. The Blessed Virgin Mary, as she was once in Cana of Galilee, is willing to carry out a thousand and one miracles if necessary for the good of our families and to help us obtain God’s grace, so that we may listen to and follow Our Lord Jesus Christ: He is the only one who has the words of eternal life.

CATHOLIC COURTSHIP

This work is to compliment the first since, in the major-ity of cases, the failure of a marriage begins in courtship.

1 GETTING TO KNOW EACH OTHER

The whole reason for the existence of Catholic courtship consists in its orientation toward a future marriage. We are not speaking about friendship between members of opposite sexes, which can be quite innocent, nor about those who play with the emotions through flirtation, which is nothing other than “playing at a loving relationship with coquetry or merely to pass the time,”81 which is no longer anything innocent. Here we are concerned with those young people who believe that they love each other and intend to formalize their relationship in marriage.

nd

2 KNOWLEDGE OF EACH OTHER

What is the characteristic of this particular relationship of courtship? Its definitive feature is that, by means of it, the couple can come to the conclusion that they are “made for each other” and that, consequently, they should, in the normal and complete way, get married in the future, with the complete conviction that they will know how, above all, to raise their future children. I say this because, throughout my pastoral experiences dealing with so many engaged couples, I have seen that thinking about raising kids is often the factor that brings people to focus on reality. Many young women who think they are in love soon realize that they should end the relationship when they think of their future children: it is often then that they realize that the young man in question is not capable of being a good father. There is also another, important way to avoid subjective whims, like the whims of those who don’t truly love the other person but are rather in love with love (that is, with what they feel): these whims lead people into error in judgments about their boyfriend or girlfriend’s suitability for starting, with minimum requisite seriousness, the great enterprise of forming “a nest for two” and for those to come. This other way is to listen to and keep in mind the opinion of one’s parents. In general, there is no love more unselfish or impartial than parental love, and, consequently, nobody is better suited to give wise and prudent advice to their children who, on account of their age and to tendency to see everything through rose-colored glasses, are often unfit to justly evaluate the suitability of the other person for a lifetime together. Furthermore, parents have greater experience in these matters: they have previously passed through this, and they know hundreds of cases of relationships among their family members, friends, and acquaintances. The courting couple must have it very clear in their minds that the end of their relationship is this knowledge of each other ordered towards marriage. This knowledge is the cause of love, since no one can love what they do not know: “love demands some apprehension of the good that is loved.”82

In other words, courtship is a preliminary state of marriage in which a certain familiarity and continuous conversation between one man and one woman must be directed to preparing for a future marriage. By preliminary, we mean that it’s not a final state, and that they’re not husband and wife yet. We know of a case of a courtship that lasted more than twenty years: the bride-to-be prepared her trousseau five times, and the groom-to-be died without ever getting married.

rd

3 LIMITED KNOWLEDGE

Reaffirming the above, I believe that a marriage which lacks the parents’ blessing is rarely—and only for serious reasons—recommended. Generally, in the short or long-run, those who get married without their parents’ blessing fail in their married life, and any exceptions “simply prove the rule.”

The mutual knowledge of the other during courtship is necessarily relative since, in a certain sense, it can only come to its total and absolute fullness in marriage. Many couples, with the excuse that they “want to get to know each other better,” engage in premarital sex, with very disastrous consequences.83 Courtship is a time of “now, but still not yet” in the relationship: they should love each other now, but not in the same way as in marriage. Growing in knowledge of each other throughout courtship should lead to mutual love, which gives rise to a spiritual union between the lover and the beloved84 since in marriage they will no longer be two but one: it is here that they should continue learning to seek the good of the other as if it were their own. The spiritual union between the souls should grow and mature throughout courtship, and only when this spiritual union is accomplished—and as a consequence of this union—should their bodies be united in marriage, thus consummating perfect unity between them. Any other alternative brings terrible consequences. If corporeal union is sought outside of marriage, there can be no true love that disinterestedly desires the good of the other; there is only an egotistical search for one’s own. If all that is sought is a mere union of bodies, how is this relationship any different from that of animals? Human love must be a love through the rational will, which orders all of the inclinations of the concupiscible appetite and must be governed by charity.

Since the couple is not yet united by the sacrament of matrimony, the relationship is dissolvable. This is why either member of the couple needs to have the courage to break up the relationship if it will not lead to a good end. Even if the couple is engaged, up to the moment of saying “I do” in the church, it is possible and even necessary—if there are reasons—to say “I don’t.” How many marriages fail because there was no courage to say “no” at the right time! I know of a case that is truly extraordinary case involving a heroic young woman: her parents firmly opposed the wedding since her fiancé was a lazy and easily angered young man. On the day of the wedding, as he took her by the arm to lead her towards the altar, she tripped on her long dress. He roughly reproached her saying, “You are always such an idiot!” When the time came for the vows, the groom gave his “I do,” but, when the priest asked the bride, “So-and-So, do you take this man to be your husband?,” her clear and serene voice could be heard, “I don’t!,” a response that was repeated when the priest asked again, amidst everyone’s astonishment. Now she is married to a different man and has several children who, when they discover what their mother did, will thank her forever and ever.

4 RESPECT WHILE GETTING TO KNOW EACH OTHER

Sadly, the criminal belief that spouses do not owe each other respect in marriage is quite widespread. Some, particularly men, suppose that everything is permitted in a marriage, which ends up killing love, since this must always be regulated by reason and made subject to the charity that prompts us to fulfill all the commandments of God’s Law. Saint Augustine, a Doctor of the Church, reproaches depraved spouses who attempt to prevent the conception of children and who, when unable to do so, have no fear of perversely destroying it, by saying, “If both man and woman are party to such practices they are not spouses at all; and if from the first they have carried on thus they have come together not for honest wedlock, but for impure gratification; if both are not party to these deeds, I make bold to say that either the one makes herself a mistress of the husband, or the other simply the paramour of his wife.”85 If the couple doesn’t learn to respect each other at the beginning of their courtship, they will respect each other even less in marriage, with foreseeable consequences. If they don’t respect each other at the moment of greatest dreams and ideals, they certainly won’t do so when devoured by routine. Paraphrasing another wellknown author, we can say that, “From an average courtship follows a bad marriage; from a good courtship, an average marriage; only from a holy courtship does a holy marriage follow.”

As a sort of piece of advice, I would say that nobody should get married without having found at least ten defects in the other, since these defects necessarily exist because of our fallen nature. If these defects haven’t been seen yet in relationship, then the couple doesn’t really know each other. Love doesn’t seek to ignore the other’s defects; rather, love helps to overcome them. If these defects aren’t revealed while courting, they will certainly appear much later, perhaps when it may be too late for a remedy. It would be vain and foolish to pretend that the other is “perfect.” If they were, it means the marriage is taking place in heaven. Not everything is rose-colored in true love. The reality is quite different. True love is crucified because it demands self-denial for the good of the other. There is no true love without the cross: the example of this was given to us by our Lord Jesus. Courtship—and marriage—doesn’t consist of adoring the other, but in one joint ascent, which, like every ascent, is difficult: “marriage is not about looking at each other, but looking together in the same direction.” We were speaking about a holy courtship, and this subsequently leads us to the most frequent danger that couples encounter, the one in which they most frequently fall.

Being young and spirited, with the love bug in their hearts, psyched up by pansexual propaganda, and at times, also by some— as Fr. All the sacrifices made to respect each other during their courtship are nothing compared to the great and many fruits that, because of those sacrifices, they will enjoy in marriage. Everything that young people do to respect each other before marriage will be appreciated in the future, since these sacrifices will overflow in the joy of their spouse, in the joy of their children, and in the joy of those who surround them. On the contrary, everything that they don’t do, instead allowing themselves to be jerked around by the winds of passion, will be the cause of bitter sadness, great disillusions, and frustrations. She loses her virginity; She feels enslaved to her boyfriend who wants to have sex more and more often; She can’t tell him no because she’s afraid that he’ll leave her, accusing her of no longer loving him; She lives in anxiety, worried that her parents will find out about what she’s doing; She shares in annoyances and troubles of sex outside of the security and peace of marriage.

Her boyfriend, on the other hand, is in no hurry to get married, since he already has all the benefits of marriage. Plus, he’s not the one who gets pregnant (at least not until now); the woman does, and this danger is so real that she can’t help but fear it.

If she does get pregnant, the woman is generally pushed towards abortion—an “unspeakable crime”90 as the Second Vatican Council calls it—which is the unjust murder of an innocent, defenseless, and unbaptized human being, and the woman will carry the guilt of having committed that cowardly act for the rest of her life.91

Furthermore, if all barriers in this relationship have already been torn down during dating, what will the woman be left with when in marriage—if that marriage even comes about—sex is sought without any regard to reason or morality? If she did not know how to respect herself or demand respect while dating, then it will be impossible for her—save a few exceptions—to be respected in marriage. If there is a wedding, it will be without joy, without excitement, without the hope of receiving or giving anything new. Later, many times she’ll hear, in the context of some marital argument, her husband’s painful reproaches incessantly reminding her of her shameful past. This is why the woman should kindly set down limits and get everything in place before the passions can speak louder than reason.

In defending the sanctity of marriage with shield and sword, the Catholic Church has done nothing else in more than twenty centuries than to defend women, “the weaker vessel”(1 Pt 3:7) and children, who are the ones who suffer the most when the divine laws that regulate marriage are ignored. Since the 1st century, the Church has been the family’s greatest defender, since she has always fought so that the woman may not be turned into a mere object of pleasure nor children into mere incubator babies.

2.

THE FREQUENCY OF ENCOUNTERS

One of the most unfortunate customs that have begun to impose themselves on relationships is the great frequency with which the couple meets. This is usually destructive because it often diminishes the newness of love, subjects it to routine, and slowly kills the excitement. For the most part, this happens because we, as a culture, have forgotten the deep meaning of rites and the profound meaning of feasts. About the former, Saint-Exupèry admirably writes, “‘It would have been better to come at the same time,’ said the fox. ‘If you come, for example, at four o’clock in the afternoon, then at three o’clock I shall begin to be happy. I shall feel happier and happier as the hour advances. At four o’clock, I shall already be worrying and jumping about. I shall show you how happy I am! But if you come at just any time, I shall never know at what hour my heart is to be ready to greet you. . . . One must observe the

‘What is a rite?’ asked the little prince.

‘Those also are actions too often neglected,’ said the fox. ‘They are what make one day different from other days, one hour from other hours. There is a rite, for example, among my hunters. Every Thursday they dance with the village girls. So Thursday is a wonderful day for me! I can take a walk as far as the vineyards. But if the hunters danced at just any time, every day would be like every other day, and I should never have any vacation at all.’”92

Regarding feasts Hans Wirtz authoritatively says, “Habit and custom are the frost of love. What we see, hear and possess daily loses its pristine, rare, and delightful shade. We end up tasting it without appreciating it, without savoring it, as if it were water. Dating couples cannot commit a greater error than being together too often. The more infrequent the encounters, the better appreciated they will be. Think of each other always; continuously yearn to be in the presence of the other, but . . . be together for the least amount of time possible. Your encounter should always be a feast.”93 Feasts cannot be celebrated every day.

How those suitors who come day after day bore the rest of the family! Quite often, the home’s intimacy is lost: the parents can’t watch television peacefully, food costs increase, even the girl-friend stops getting properly fixed-up, they sometimes do not finish their studies and, what’s worse, they lose contact with their own friends. The relationship of a dating couple should be gradual, relaxed, and should leave time for getting to know each other in a mature and serious way. That is why couples should begin as acquaintances, then as friends, afterwards as showing interest, and then once they have chosen each other, as “filo” (as it used to be said, from the popular Italian filare: to woo, to court94). Up until this point, no decision has been made. Only much later are they engaged, when the man enters her home to “ask for her hand,” and in this way he brings about the mutual promise of fidelity and future marriage, once the character and endowments (physical, psychological, moral, cultural, and religious) of the other has been determined, in order to see if they can be adapted to the other. To “ask for her hand” is a beautiful expression that means that the young man intends to make this particular woman his spouse.

To those who frequently meet in isolated and, more often than not, dark places: the Word of God teaches, “Flee from sin as from a serpent” (Sir 21:2), of which Saint Isidore comments, “It is impossible to be near the serpent and remain a long time without getting bitten.”95

It is certain that “those who love danger will perish in it.” (Sir 3:27) since the occasion makes the thief; and if the couple often meet—I speak of the majority of cases—in isolated and dark places, they are putting themselves in the occasion of sin. Thus, as Saint Bernard says, “To be always in a woman’s company without having carnal knowledge of her [we could add, in a man’s company without knowledge of him] - is this not a greater miracle than raising the dead? You cannot perform the lesser feat; do you expect me to believe that you can do the greater?”96 It must be very clear that those who are courting have no right to the pleasures of the flesh which, consummated or not, are sinful. This is not the case in marriage.

3.

THE PARENTS’ CONCERN

The parents should advise their children regarding their relationships. To do this, the parents need to find out about the prospective candidate and about his or her family, discretely controlling their child’s interactions with the beloved, spacing out their visits, reminding them of their obligations and duties of their state of life, without removing their excitement but making them come back down to earth and make contact with reality.

Saint Alphonsus Liguori says gravely, “Certain fathers and foolish mothers knowingly allow their sons to frequent bad company and houses in which there are young females, and permit their daughters to be alone with men. They endeavor to justify the neglect of their children by saying: ‘I do not wish to entertain bad thoughts of others.’ O folly of parents! They are in such cases bound to suspect the evil which may happen; and, in order to prevent it, they should correct their children.”97

Parents should act in this way not because they distrust their children, but because they are acquainted with human nature, fallen because of original sin; they know that their children do not know everything and, as a result, may not be able to defend themselves against those impending dangers.

AGE

Father, what’s the right age to start dating? This is a question that we hear often and to which we invariably respond:

Love has no age: we know of very happy marriages of couples who began dating at a young age, but also of those who met at a much older age.

In general, it’s not a good idea to begin dating at too young of an age for several reasons:

1. Young people lack the maturity that comes with age.

2. They lack responsibility.

3. The prospect of a necessarily long courtship is always dangerous; love can grow cold if too much time passes.

4. They quite literally lose the best years of their youth in addition to losing relationships with their friends, male or female, which is very important for life in general.

5. Many times, young people lose interest in a career or professional development when they begin dating.

6. When someone is very young, the field for selecting a boyfriend or girlfriend is necessarily limited. With the years, one’s circle of acquaintances and friends broadens, and the selection can be better made.

The obsession that many fourteen year old girls have for obtaining a boyfriend is very harmful. They think that without a boyfriend now, they’ll end up single: this is the effect of so many soap operas!

They haven’t even stopped playing with dolls when sometimes their own mothers push them into a relationship!

The nature of things must be respected. Relationships grow like fruit: they need time to mature, but if they are not picked at the proper time, they fall and rot. Likewise, if courtship not been given its required time, the marriage will still be green and immature. If the courtship is mature, and yet the marriage isn’t carried out, the relationship usually decays and breaks down. Consequently, it’s a good idea not to rush the engagement, but not to allow the opportune time to pass away, which is what happens to those who begin their courtship at too young of an age.

Finally, we must accentuate that the big differences between men and women—economical, cultural, of age, of religion—are generally an obstacle that contributes to the failure of a marriage. The spouses should be, in a certain sense, similar to each other, since likeness is the cause of love. Saint Thomas Aquinas teaches that two are alike inasmuch as they actually possess the same quality; they are one in that form. Hence the affections of one tend to the other as to himself, and the one desires the good of the other as his own.98 A courting couple will be happy in marriage only if their love is this way, and in this way the effects of love will come about: union, mutual indwelling, that is, when the lover is said to be in the beloved and vice-versa, ecstasy, that is, coming out of one’s self to procure the good of the other (this is the opposite of egoism, which is to enclose oneself in oneself), and jealousy (not the jealousy of envy, but one that seeks to repel all obstacles that are contrary to love). Love causes a wound in the one who loves, which impels him to always labor motivated by love.99

4.

THE RELIGIOUS DIMENSION OF COURTSHIP

What is the best way to know if the members of a couple really and truly love each other? What sign is there that their love is true and sincere? The certain sign that they are in love is the growth of their love for God. It’s a sure sign that a marriage will fail if the couple doesn’t love God during the courtship; a relationship where God is loved only as an excuse to love each other is a sign of an unstable and easily-broken marriage in the future. On the contrary, a relationship where God is loved above all things is a sign that they will have a solid marriage, “founded upon rock” (Mt 7:25). The rain of difficulties will fall, torrents of sacrifices will come, winds of calamities will blow, but the marriage will remain standing. A failure to love God “with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, with all your strength” (Mk 12:30), is the first and foremost cause of the failures of marriages. When God is the “stone guest”

in the home, little by little, the hearts of its members will also become stone (cf Ez 36:26).100 On the other hand, when all of the family’s members fulfill that “greatest and first commandment” (Mt 22:38), they realize that:

there is no problem without solution, there is no day without joy, there is no work without merit, there is no cross without consolation, there is no labor without satisfaction.

Today, many people are miserable because they haven’t followed God’s will. God calls them to something greater, more sublime, but they pretended to be deaf and followed their own desires, ceaselessly finding consolation for their painful erring. Hence, whoever truly wants God to reign in their courtship and later in their marriage, should first be willing to follow the vocation that God wants for them. If God wants a young man to be a priest, he will never be happy in marriage and, furthermore, his wife and his children won’t be happy either. If a young lady does not follow Christ’s call to be His spouse, she will be always walking far from happiness. Everybody recognizes that if God calls you to marriage, you won’t be happy as a monk, but very few can see that the reverse is also true. Once we know that God wants us to be married, we have to choose our spouse according to His design: this is why we constantly need to always pray for the husband or wife that God has destined for us, as well as for our children.

In addition, the couple should form themselves by examining together the true meaning of marriage, along with its duties and rights. They should understand the Catholic doctrine, reading the pontifical documents about the topic, such as Pius XI’s encyclical Casti Connubii, Gaudium et Spes, the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, no. 46—52, Paul VI’s Humanae Vi-tae, Pope Saint John Paul II’s Familiaris Consortio, and others. They should also read good books such as Fulton Sheen’s Three to Get Married, Raúl Plus’s Christ in the Home, Karol Wojtyla’s Love and Re-sponsibility, and the like. They should also become more cultured by developing good taste in music, refined theatre, world literature and the literature of their country, and art. They should dedicate themselves to apostolic works, even as part of associations or organized groups, helping in parishes, chapels, or movements, giving to others that which they have received from Christ, and why not? In so far as it is possible, they should engage in some works of mercy like visiting hospitals, hospices, nursing homes. In short, the couple should cultivate the intellect by adhering to the truth, the will by practicing charity—which helps them to come out of themselves— and the sensibility by forming good taste in beauty.

In conclusion, hold on to those dreams and ideals of your childhood, the dream of having a home unlike any other in the world. Know that God Himself associates spouses with Him as co-creators in His masterpiece. Understand that Jesus Christ needs you as teachers, guides, and priests in this “domestic Church,”101 which is the Catholic family. Know that you are destined for one of the holiest, most praiseworthy, and most meritorious of works: the begetting of children for the Church, citizens for the nation, and saints for Heaven. Knead your relationship with prayer, frequent reception of the sacraments, participation in Sunday Mass, tender devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and reading of the Word of God, fidelity to the Church, a personal interaction with the saints to whom you are devoted, and in this way, sanctifying yourself more and more each day. Here we can say that “the family that prays together stays together.”

We Catholic priests have the great grace of meeting young people of both sexes who are models of chastity. Some—far more than what people and the Kinsey Reports say—have never stained their souls with any sin of impurity. By conserving their baptismal innocence, these will forge the most solid, fertile, and joyful homes. Satanic propaganda seeks to drag all youth into the darkness of impurity, saying even that “all men are the same” or that “all women are the same,” something completely and utterly false. I can assure young people that there are many who will be great fathers of families and many heroines in their home for having practiced chastity in an exemplary way. In the end, with God’s grace, we will continue to meet fathers and mothers, loving husbands and wives, who, like beautiful flowers, will continue to shine even in the worst moral swamps for the honor and esteem of the Church and of their nation.

Jesus Christ “is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Heb 13:8) and will continue to raise up holy couples who will follow Him with all their love and fidelity because He is the only one who has “the words of eternal life” (Jn 6:68).

SOME CLARIFICATIONS REGARDING PEDOPHILIA

By Fr. Miguel Ángel Fuentes, IVE

In 2001, the problem of pedophilia among members of the Catholic clergy and religious in the United States jumped to the front pages of the newspapers, likely constituting one of the greatest scandals of the century. The news was scandalous even though, properly speaking, in many cases the events reported had transpired several decades before. Without letting off completely, interest in the topic dwindled for some years before returning to occupy journalists’ pens in 2008: this time the stage was European, principally in Ireland and Germany, but with incidents in other countries as well. Setting aside a final judgment about this situation, which has not yet reached its conclusion, let us at least say that the media coverage of these events has been, to put it charitably, notably inaccurate and even incompetent. Since a great deal of confusion has resulted from the media’s coverage, confusion experienced by both Catholics and non-Catholics alike, I think some clarifications are in order.

1. The Seriousness: First and foremost, so as to avoid any misinterpretation, pedophilia or paedophilia is objectively one of the gravest of human depravities, and is absolutely unjustifiable in any situation imaginable. This is because of the condition of the victim, who is the child, and because of the presumed degeneration of the perpetrator. This is even truer if the perpetrator is a priest: if the perpetrator is still in a state where he acts with complete freedom, pedophilia is a sin that cries out to heaven. It is not the most serious of all sins, since abortion and infanticide, which involve the murder of unborn or newborn children at hands of their own parents, who, ironically, claim to be acting at the service of human life and health, are certainly more serious.

2. The Nature: the term pedophilia (or paedophilia) comes from the Greek paidós, meaning “child,” and filia, meaning “friendship.” The word paidophilia was coined by Greek poets as a substitute for “pederasty” (from paidós, child and erastos, lover).102

According to the DSM-IV, pedophilia is a paraphilia, defined by experiencing “recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, sexual urges, or behaviors . . . that occur over a period of six months.” Beyond this general definition, pedophilia “involves sexual activity with a prepubescent child (generally age 13 years or younger).” Again, to be considered pedophilia, properly speaking, the attractions must have occurred “over a period of six months” (otherwise, the attractions might be considered as a fleeting temptation), and that the affected individual “must age 16 years or older and at least 5 years older than the child.”103

For its part, the ICD-10 says that it is “a sexual preference for children, usually of prepubertal or early pubertal age. Some paedophiles are attracted only to girls, others only to boys, and others again are interested in both sexes. Paedophilia is rarely identified in women. . . . An isolated incident, especially if the perpetrator is himself an adolescent, does not establish the presence of the persistent or predominant tendency required for the diagnosis.”104

Hence, a dominant characteristic of pedophilia is a persistent or a predominant sexual preference for children; this is why many professionals, and even the ICD-10, don’t consider pedophilia, properly speaking, as the disorder which affects those who abuse children but without a predominant preference for them.105 Of course, even if this abuse is not pedophilia, properly speaking, which is a psychological deviation, we have a person with greater freedom and responsibility, and hence his crime is all the more serious.

3. The Specifics: It follows, then, that, strictly speaking, pedophilia is not a predominant sexual preference for teenagers, as was the case in many of the incidents that the press erroneously termed pedophilia; rather, this preference for teenagers should be termed ephebophilia (from ephebus, meaning teenager or young man). Neither is pedophilia a general homosexual attraction that is occasionally directed to a child in the absence of an adult or adolescent subject: this is, rather, homosexuality and the occasional molestation of minors, and many of the incidents that the media poorly portrayed as paedophilia actually fall under this heading. Both behaviors (ephebophilia and homosexuality) are highly reprehensible from a moral point of view as well as from a civil and canonical perspective. Since they involved minors, they also constitute serious crimes, but these incidents are of psychological nature different from that of pedophilia.

4. In Latin America, Brazil has the worst record, with nearly two million child and adolescent prostitutes.110

A combined analysis finds that there are more than 10 million children involved in the world of prostitution, the sex industry, and

child sexual abuse and child sexual assault; 4) poverty; 5) the presence of large child pornography.111 The data provided in 2009 by the International Observatory against Online Child Abuse and Sexual Exploitation gives the following statistics:112 In 2009, there were 49,393 pedophilic sites based in 35 countries.

The statistics that Ciccone cites, however, highlight not simply the numbers but rather the nature of pedophilia in our days: what is new is pedophilia’s form of social organization, and not so much the mental structure that sustains it, which has always existed. Likewise adults were represented as pseudo-children 792 times. All this, said Reisman, is an “education” that much of the society has been receiving for more than three decades, and its main message is as follows: children are seductive and are hungry for sex. One of the most significant according to Reisman is the use of pseudochildren: half-naked women with children’s characteristics (surrounded by dolls, plush Teddy bears, baby shoes, baby bottles, toys, etc.), adults in diapers in the fetal position in a rocking chair and with their thumb in their mouths, or cast in scenes from fairy tales. The researcher thinks that this corresponds to the explicit intention to awaken pedophilic sexual stimuli, even in those who do not suffer this type of perversion. Even though it is not pedophilia, what must also be mentioned as a significant factor and as guilty by association with the phenomenon of child corruption, and, therefore, child sexual abuse, are the proposals for reducing school sex education to a mere giving of information about functions and possible uses of the genitals. In this way, rather than teaching children about their affections, love, and self-control, it awakens the curiosity of children and adolescents, undermines their consciences by calling evil good and good evil, and encourages them to use their sexuality “safely,” with a safety that is questionable or doubtful, and well as morally illicit.

5. Causes: It is very difficult to establish the causes of the problem of pedophilia, as is also the case with the rest of the paraphilias among which it is listed in the ICD-10 and DSM-IV (the manual that, under pressure from special interest groups, removed homosex-uality from the list of diseases in 1973). For those who give explanations of paraphilias with purely psychiatric categories (e.g., Krafft-Ebing and Kraepelin), pedophilia is caused by an alteration of the purpose of the sex drive; it was these who coined the expression “psychopathic degeneration.” Freud and his school allude to a disruption in psychological development during a lower stage and the replacement of a real, more or less symbolized object for the natural one. The positivists-behaviorists (e.g., Kinsey, Masters, Johnson, and Kaplan) explained the phenomenon by the laws of the “stimulus and response.” Other theories try to interpret the phenomenon in terms of the endocrine system (hyper- or hyposexuality).116 Lastly, still others attribute them to the confluence of several causes. For example, H. Bless considers it as having an internal psychopathic basis or tendency favored by external circumstances, that is, a particular environment: a defective psychosexual development (remaining in an early or infantile stage of the sexual life, since children’s forms are always an auto-erotic) and external triggers (bad habits, viewing pornography, the abuse of alcohol and drugs, Cybersex, etc.).117

A subject who is not mentally ill might also experience passing pedophilic attractions, especially if they live out their sexuality in a disorderly manner; however, this does not constitute pedophilia, and nor does it follow that the person has some other sort of perversion. Rather, these attractions can be explained by two closely linked causes: (a) on the one hand, the deep disappointment that sex produces when it is used outside of the context of true love (masturbation, fornication, prostitution, adultery, homosexuality, etc.). In these cases, it often pushes the subject to seek more intense and bizarre experiences in an effort to achieve a sexual ecstasy that lust promises but cannot deliver; (b) on the other hand, there is the incessant bombardment of pornography that, through child sexual propaganda, aims to awaken not only illicit but also perverted passions.118 The subject’s action would still, in this case, be criminal, although it will not be from the psychological disturbance of pedophilia.

6. Disease or Vice? The question then arises of those who truly are pedophiles and who repeatedly commit acts of pedophilia: are pedophiles simply sick people, or are they criminals, or are they a little bit of both? To what degree are they responsible? The true pedophile has a serious psychological problem, but the there is no way to determine the degree of his responsibility a priori, since this depends on the level of compulsivity that their obsession has reached and the causes that have led to the appearance of this phenomenon in the affected person. A pedophile is responsible for their actions to the extent that: (a) they are aware of their perversion and damage that it is capable of causing, (b) and that they are able to prevent the carrying out of those acts or at least avoid situations that give rise to their compulsions, or understand that they must seek professional help.

Generally the Church considers that, in many cases, there is responsibility, and, in some cases, it may be very serious.119 Nevertheless, the Church does not deny that, in many instances, especially when dealing with irrepressible instincts and deviations or some psychotic alienation of personality (such as a depersonalization or dissociative disorder), the degree of responsibility becomes more doubtful.120

7. Can the damage caused by pedophiles be prevented?

For all of the deviations that affect the innocent, the most important concern is prevention. No matter what specific responsibilities a sick subject might have, society has an obligation to protect its members, especially the most vulnerable. 5. Faced with this world the Church steps up as a “sign of contradiction”

Who, unless assisted by supernatural help, would oppose such an unstoppable avalanche? Without God’s help, who would give a witness different from what the world likes and wants to hear? How can we not realize that this firmness of doctrine provokes hatred from those who live controlled by their passions? Is this not one of the main reasons that they seek to silence the Catholic Church, so that she would not teach what God has revealed in the Bible? How can they not campaign against the buffets contemporary hedonism receives from virginity and celibacy? How can they not take psychological action against virginity and celibacy, minutely investigating anomalies—real or imaginary—in order to justify themselves? Can it be that today, as yesterday, it is the very “nature of man, inclined to vice, which wants to show that it not only has license, but also reason to sin,” seeking to justify itself with the evil deeds— real or imaginary—of others?153

As a result of this lack of historical perspective, we are not aware of the seriousness of what is happening at our time in history, just as the Romans in their times were not aware that vomiting in order to continue to eat was corrupt. With time, we become aware and condemn these practices and the current caricatures of true human love will be seen in the same way. The Church will rise like a standard over the nations for having been alone in coming out in defense of authentic love. Similarly, the consecrated virgins and those who remain celibate for the kingdom of Heaven, who do not give in, in spite of the destructive psychological pressures against them, will be considered heroes. They remained largely faithful, writing one of the most beautiful pages of the history of the Church and of the world. “In spite of painful negative cases,”154 total consecration to God shines stronger and more beautifully than ever. Think of John Paul II, Mother Teresa of Calcutta, or the holy Padre Pio and the thousands of blesseds and saints raised to the honor of the altars in the last decades and in all of the history of the Church!

Benedict Groeschel155 took upon himself the work of putting together a statistic. 6. Lastly, it is an attack against the Pope

The vicious attacks on human love and celibacy are aimed, indirectly but truly, against the Pope, who is the firm defender of the truth regarding human love, virginity and ecclesiastic celibacy.

Here are three examples that show the serious discrimination suffered by the Pope from the mass media:

1. Every technological advance that allows Professor Stephen Hawking to continue working from his wheel chair, communicating through a sophisticated system, is euphorically applauded. When the Pope used the Pope-mobile or a moving platform, some asked that he be removed from office. His inability was ridiculed and, in his sickness, he was attacked for what he taught and what he bore witness to.157

Dear Youth:

This is only a part of what the Pope has to pay for his valiant defense of the truth of human love and for being the Vicar of Jesus Christ.

“In spite of painful negative cases,”160 even in our own celibate lives, we will also have to pay something for announcing, celebrating, and witnessing to the truth of human love and being faithful to Jesus Christ.

The world can defile human love more and more, but we will always have the witness of thousands and thousands of our brothers and sisters who, in the beautiful saying of Saint Augustine, “aged virgins”161 because they truly gave themselves for the love of Jesus Christ. May the Virgin Mary encourage us to rejoice in the Church of her Son who will be set up as a signal for the peoples (Is 11:10).
